title: Beyond Cisco: The Enterprise Networking Market in 2026
excerpt: Two 2025 deals redrew the map: HPE now owns Juniper and Arista owns VeloCloud. Part 1 of a vendor-neutral, 19-vendor analysis — who really competes with Cisco, and in which category.
author: Rupesh Kumar
content:
If you are refreshing a network, renewing a Cisco Enterprise Agreement or writing an RFP this year, the shortlist you used in 2024 is probably out of date. This series is the result of a structured, vendor-neutral study of **19 networking and security vendors**, benchmarked against Cisco across portfolio, licensing, pricing, five-year total cost of ownership and regional fit in **India, Europe and the United States**.

**In this part:** what changed in 2025, the headline answers, and who competes in which category.

> **Key takeaways**
> - The market has consolidated: **HPE completed its US$14bn acquisition of Juniper (2 July 2025)** and **Arista acquired VeloCloud SD-WAN from Broadcom (1 July 2025)**.
> - **HPE Networking (Aruba + Juniper)** is now the only competitor matching Cisco across every major domain.
> - In the modelled 500-user campus, Cisco's 5-year TCO is the highest of the enterprise-grade stacks; Fortinet's is the lowest.

## What changed in 2025

The enterprise networking market in 2026 has consolidated around a
handful of full-stack platforms. Two 2025 transactions reshaped the
competitive map against Cisco: **HPE completed its US$14 billion
acquisition of Juniper Networks on 2 July 2025**, doubling HPE's
networking business and adding routing, data-center switching and
firewalls to the Aruba campus/WLAN portfolio; and **Arista acquired the
VeloCloud SD-WAN business from Broadcom (closed 1 July 2025)**, giving
Arista a WAN/branch offer to sit beside its data-center and campus
switching. Broadcom's VMware unit has therefore exited SD-WAN and is now
relevant only for NSX data-center network virtualisation inside VMware
Cloud Foundation.

The practical consequence: any vendor comparison written before mid-2025 needs to be re-baselined. "Juniper vs Aruba" is now one company's roadmap question, and VMware is no longer an SD-WAN option.

## The headline answers

| **Question**                                  | **Short answer**                                                                          | **Why**                                                                                                                                                  |
|-----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Strongest overall Cisco alternative           | HPE Networking (Aruba + Juniper)                                                          | Only competitor with campus, WLAN, SD-WAN, SSE, routing, DC fabric and firewalls under one owner; strong AIOps (Mist, Central).                          |
| Best price/performance                        | Fortinet (campus/branch/security); Arista (data center)                                   | Fortinet's ASIC-based FortiGate bundles security + SD-WAN in one licence; Arista leads DC throughput per dollar and operational simplicity.              |
| Lowest modelled 5-year TCO (enterprise-grade) | Fortinet (Huawei similar where it can be procured)                                        | Lowest subscription load per device and single-OS operations; see Part 4.                                                                            |
| Strongest SD-WAN                              | Fortinet, Cisco (Catalyst SD-WAN/Meraki), HPE EdgeConnect, Palo Alto Prisma SD-WAN, Versa | All are long-running Gartner SD-WAN Leaders; Fortinet best for security-led branches, HPE EdgeConnect for WAN optimisation, Versa for service providers. |
| Strongest data-center networking              | Arista; Cisco Nexus/ACI and Juniper (Apstra/QFX) close behind                             | EOS single image, CloudVision, 400G/800G AI fabrics, very low defect rates.                                                                              |
| Strongest WLAN/campus                         | HPE (Aruba + Juniper Mist), Cisco                                                         | AI-driven assurance, Wi-Fi 7 portfolios, mature NAC (ClearPass / ISE).                                                                                   |
| Strongest security ecosystem                  | Palo Alto Networks; Fortinet; Cisco (with Splunk)                                         | Threat-prevention depth (PAN), integrated fabric (Fortinet), SOC/XDR breadth (Cisco + Splunk).                                                           |
| Best automation/AIOps                         | Juniper Mist (Marvis) and Arista CloudVision                                              | Most mature AI-assisted troubleshooting and state-streaming automation.                                                                                  |
| Strongest in India                            | Cisco (installed base), then HPE Aruba, Fortinet                                          | Cisco dominates BFSI/government/IT-ITES; Fortinet and Aruba gain on cost; Huawei restricted in telecom.                                                  |
| Strongest in Europe                           | Cisco, HPE (Aruba + Juniper), Fortinet; Nokia/Ericsson in carriers                        | Broad partner coverage; Huawei restricted in many EU 5G/critical networks.                                                                               |
| Strongest in the US                           | Cisco; Arista in DC; Palo Alto in security                                                | Federal certifications, largest partner base, hyperscaler adoption of Arista.                                                                            |
| Best for global enterprise                    | Cisco or HPE Networking                                                                   | Global depot/RMA, local TAC, consistent licensing worldwide.                                                                                             |
| Best for telecom                              | Nokia, Juniper (HPE), Cisco; Ciena for optical                                            | SR-MPLS/SRv6 routing scale, IP/optical convergence; Huawei restricted by India 'trusted source' and EU 5G Toolbox rules.                                 |
| Best for cost-sensitive organisations         | Fortinet (security-led); Ubiquiti/MikroTik for SMB only                                   | Lowest acquisition cost; accept reduced support depth below enterprise grade.                                                                            |
| New enterprise network today                  | Single-vendor campus/branch + best-of-breed DC + converged SASE                           | Typical answer: HPE or Cisco for campus/WLAN, Arista for DC, Fortinet or Palo Alto for security/SASE — validated per region.                             |

## Five-year TCO snapshot (500-user campus)

The single most-asked question is cost. Here is the modelled five-year TCO for a medium campus (Scenario B, US pricing, excluding tax) — the full model is in [Part 4](/hub/enterprise-network-vendors-2026-five-year-tco).

Fortinet ≈ $0.52M · Huawei\* ≈ $0.53M · Extreme + FortiGate ≈ $0.59M
· HPE ≈ $0.65M · Arista + partner NGFW ≈ $0.67M · Cisco ≈ $0.76M.
Cisco carries the highest TCO in every scenario, typically 25–45% above
the lowest enterprise-grade option (Fortinet) and ~15–18% above HPE, but
also the lowest migration risk for Cisco-skilled teams. \*Huawei is
shown for reference only; it is restricted or politically difficult in
the US, much of Europe and Indian telecom networks.

The Cisco premium is real, but so is what it buys: skills availability, ecosystem breadth and the lowest migration risk for teams that already run Cisco.

### What the analysts said (2025)

Analyst signals (2025): Gartner's 2025 Magic Quadrant for Enterprise
Wired and Wireless LAN Infrastructure (25 June 2025) named Huawei a
Leader for a third year as the only non-North American Leader; listings
also show HPE (Aruba), Juniper and Fortinet as Leaders. The 2024 SD-WAN
Magic Quadrant Leaders were Broadcom (VeloCloud), Cisco, Fortinet, HPE,
Palo Alto Networks and Versa. The 9 July 2025 SASE Platforms Magic
Quadrant Leaders announced by vendors include Palo Alto Networks (third
consecutive year), Fortinet, Cato Networks and Netskope.

## How this analysis was built

- Sources prioritised: vendor documentation and datasheets,
  vendor/partner price pages, authorised resellers (CDW, SHI, Ubiquiti
  store), Gartner Magic Quadrant announcements (2024–2025), and
  reputable trade press. Sources and dates are listed in the Appendix.

- Most enterprise vendors (Cisco Catalyst, Juniper, Arista, Huawei,
  Nokia, Extreme) do not publish full price lists; where so, figures are
  labelled **Market estimate** or **Enterprise quote**.

- TCO uses a transparent bottom-up model: hardware, optics, spares,
  installation/professional services, training, licences/subscriptions,
  support, security services, NAC, SASE, management platform and
  operations labour, with 4% annual subscription escalation from Year 2.

- Scores (1–10) are the author's analytical judgement informed by the
  research; they should be recalibrated with the organisation's own
  weights.

The rest of the series goes deeper: products and features, licensing, cost, regional fit, and finally how to choose, migrate and negotiate.

*Research date: 8 October 2026. Vendor-neutral and independent — no vendor sponsorship. Prices, licences and product names change frequently; re-validate every figure with at least two authorised partners per region before purchasing. TCO figures are illustrative models built on stated assumptions, not quotations. Gartner content is cited via vendor and press announcements. Not legal, tax or investment advice.*

author: Rupesh Kumar
content:
Feature lists are where vendor comparisons usually get vague. This part puts the major product families side by side, then compares capabilities on one matrix so you can see what is native, what needs a licence and what needs another vendor.

> **Key takeaways**
> - Only **Cisco** and **HPE Networking (Aruba + Juniper)** cover campus, WLAN, SD-WAN, SASE, routing, data center and firewall with first-party products.
> - **Arista, Extreme and Dell** need a partner for NGFW/SSE; **Palo Alto, Check Point, Cato and Zscaler** are security/SASE specialists, not LAN vendors.
> - Most "advanced" capabilities — SDN fabrics, SD-WAN, zero trust, AIOps — sit behind **licensed tiers**, which matters for [licensing and TCO](/hub/enterprise-network-vendors-2026-licensing-and-pricing).

## What I'd take from this

- **Protocol choice drives lock-in.** EIGRP, TrustSec/SGT and ACI contracts are Cisco-specific; designs built on OSPF/BGP, EVPN-VXLAN and RADIUS keep every domain replaceable.
- **"Supported" is not "included".** Check whether a capability is in the base OS or a subscription tier before comparing hardware prices.
- **Automation maturity varies widely.** Arista (eAPI, gNMI, AVD), Juniper (NETCONF-native, Apstra) and Nokia (gNMI-first) stand out for NetDevOps teams.

title: Network Licensing Decoded: Cisco vs Competitors on Licences, Prices and Support
excerpt: Hardware ≠ licence ≠ cloud management ≠ support ≠ security subscription. How Cisco, HPE, Juniper, Arista, Fortinet, Palo Alto and others really charge — with real reseller prices from October 2026.
author: Rupesh Kumar
content:
The hardware price on a quote is rarely the number that matters. Over five years, subscriptions, cloud management, support and security services usually outweigh the box itself. This part breaks down how each vendor charges, with real reseller prices captured on 8 October 2026.

> **Key takeaways**
> - Treat **hardware, software licence, cloud management, support and security subscription as five separate line items** — bundles hide the split.
> - Cisco Catalyst 9000 orders require a **3-, 5- or 7-year term subscription** on top of the perpetual licence; renewals are the largest Cisco campus OPEX lever.
> - Meraki, Aruba Central (AOS-10 APs) and Mist APs **need an active cloud licence** to keep working — budget them as mandatory OPEX.

> **How to read prices in this series.** *Confirmed / Public MSRP* = published by the vendor or a named reseller's list price. *Reseller price* = advertised by a named authorised reseller on 8 October 2026. *Market estimate* = my street-price range for budgeting. *Enterprise quote* = not publicly disclosed; large deals typically land 30–60% below list. Planning rates: USD 1 = INR 95 = EUR 0.87.

## The rule for every evaluation

Rule for every evaluation: **Hardware cost ≠ Software licence ≠ Cloud
management ≠ Support ≠ Security subscription.** Each is a separate line
item, has a separate term, and is renewed (or not) independently. Many
vendors bundle them on a single SKU for convenience, which hides the
split.

## Cisco licensing in detail

| **Network Stack (Network Essentials / Network Advantage)**     | Perpetual licence tied to Catalyst 9000 hardware; Essentials covers L2/basic L3, Advantage adds full routing, VRF, MPLS/EVPN, etc.                                                                   | Choose tier up front; upgrading later costs more than buying Advantage at purchase for distribution/core. |

Renewal pricing is the largest Cisco campus OPEX lever.              |

## Practical advice

- **Buy the right Cisco tier up front.** Upgrading from Network Essentials to Advantage later costs more than buying Advantage for distribution/core at purchase.
- **Model renewals, not just year one.** Palo Alto subscriptions can reach 3–4× the appliance cost over five years; negotiate renewal caps.
- **Watch optics.** Vendor-branded optics run 3–10× third-party; ask for a fixed optics price list or third-party optics support.

excerpt: A transparent bottom-up TCO model — from a 50-user branch to a 10,000-user global enterprise — comparing Cisco, HPE, Arista, Fortinet, Extreme, Huawei and Ubiquiti. Hardware is the smallest part of the bill.
author: Rupesh Kumar
content:
"Which vendor is cheapest?" depends on the size of the estate and on what you count. This part uses a transparent, bottom-up model to compare five-year total cost of ownership across four realistic scenarios — and shows why the lowest hardware price rarely wins.

> **Key takeaways**
> - **Hardware is the smallest part of TCO** above branch size; subscriptions, support, NAC/SASE and operations labour dominate.
> - **Cisco carries the highest TCO in every scenario**, about 25–45% above Fortinet (the lowest enterprise-grade stack) and ~15–18% above HPE.
> - **Negotiating renewal caps is worth more than the upfront discount**, because recurring costs are ~45–55% of five-year TCO before labour.

> **How to read prices in this series.** *Confirmed / Public MSRP* = published by the vendor or a named reseller's list price. *Reseller price* = advertised by a named authorised reseller on 8 October 2026. *Market estimate* = my street-price range for budgeting. *Enterprise quote* = not publicly disclosed; large deals typically land 30–60% below list. Planning rates: USD 1 = INR 95 = EUR 0.87.

| **IGST / GST**                          | 18%                                                                                                                                | Recoverable as input tax credit for GST-registered enterprises; a real cost for exempt entities (some government, education, healthcare).                                                            |
| **Distributor + SI margin**             | 8–20% combined                                                                                                                     | Major distributors: Ingram Micro India, Redington, Savex, iValue, Rashi; SIs: TCS, Wipro, HCLTech, Tech Mahindra, Dimension Data/NTT, Sify, Orange Business, Comtel, Locuz, Embee.                   |

| **Government / PSU procurement**        | GeM portal, L1 tendering, PMA (Preferential Market Access) and Make-in-India local-content norms; Trusted Source rules for telecom | Huawei/ZTE are not designated trusted sources for telecom networks; many government bodies avoid Chinese vendors entirely.                                                                           |

### Market analysis

| **Dimension**                           | **Assessment**                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Most commonly deployed (enterprise)** | Cisco (clear #1 installed base), HPE Aruba, Fortinet (firewall/SD-WAN #1 by units), Juniper, Palo Alto, Check Point; Ruckus in hospitality/education; D-Link, TP-Link Omada, Netgear in SMB. |
| **Telecom**                             | Nokia, Ericsson, Samsung (RAN), Cisco, Juniper, Ciena (optical/IP); Huawei/ZTE limited to legacy since 2021 trusted-source mandate.                                                            |
| **BFSI**                                | Cisco + Palo Alto/Check Point/Fortinet dominate (RBI cybersecurity framework, SEBI CSCRF); Arista growing in DC; Aruba/Juniper Mist in branch WLAN.                                            |
| **Government**                          | Cisco, HPE, Juniper; growing preference for Make-in-India and indigenous (e.g., C-DOT, Tejas, Sterlite/STL) in telecom/defence.                                                                |
| **Manufacturing**                       | Cisco IE (industrial Ethernet), Fortinet OT security, HPE Aruba, Siemens/Moxa/Hirschmann for OT.                                                                                               |
| **IT/ITES**                             | Cisco, Arista (DC), Palo Alto, Zscaler (SSE), Fortinet; GCCs often mirror their HQ vendor standards.                                                                                           |
| **Partner ecosystem**                   | Deepest: Cisco \> HPE Aruba ≈ Fortinet \> Juniper \> Palo Alto \> Arista \> Extreme.                                                                                                           |
| **Certified engineers**                 | CCNA/CCNP very abundant; Fortinet NSE strong; Juniper JNCIA/JNCIS moderate; Aruba ACMP moderate; Arista ACE scarce.                                                                            |
| **Support quality**                     | Cisco/Juniper/HPE have India TAC centres (Bengaluru); 4-hr depot coverage strong in Tier-1 cities, weaker in Tier-3.                                                                           |
| **Training**                            | Abundant Cisco/Fortinet academies; Juniper and Aruba education partners in major metros.                                                                                                       |

### Vendors with lower TCO in India

- **Fortinet** — single FortiGate licence covering NGFW + SD-WAN,
  FortiSwitch/FortiAP without per-device cloud fees when managed from
  FortiGate; strong local partner base.

- **HPE Aruba (Instant On for SMB; CX/AOS-10 for enterprise)** —
  lifetime hardware warranty on many models reduces AMC; aggressive
  India discounting.

- **Juniper Mist** — lower operational labour through AI-driven
  troubleshooting; competitive pricing in BFSI WLAN tenders.

- **Ruckus, D-Link/TP-Link Omada, Ubiquiti** — for SMB, hospitality and
  education where enterprise TAC is not mandatory.

- Labour is cheaper in India (modelled at ~25% of US cost), so
  subscriptions and hardware form a larger share of TCO than in the US —
  making licence negotiation the biggest lever.

AMC (Annual Maintenance Contract) in India is often delivered by the system integrator on top of OEM support at 6–12% of hardware value per year — budget both OEM back-to-back support and SI AMC.

## Europe

| **Dimension**                | **Assessment**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **EUR pricing**              | Most vendors publish EUR price lists to partners; EUR list is often ~equal to USD list numerically, i.e., ~10–15% dearer after FX. Example: Aruba Central Advanced 3-yr (JZ526AAE) €702 street (MSRP €890) vs $766 (MSRP $950) in the US (SHI, Oct 2026).           |
| **VAT**                      | 17% (LU) to 27% (HU); 19% DE, 20% FR/UK, 21% NL/ES, 22% IT. Recoverable for VAT-registered businesses.                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Import/logistics**         | Most network equipment is 0% duty under the WTO ITA; main cost is intra-EU logistics and WEEE compliance.                                                                                                                                                             |
| **GDPR / data residency**    | Cloud-managed platforms (Meraki, Central, Mist, CVaaS, ExtremeCloud IQ, FortiCloud) all offer EU-hosted regions; verify telemetry/PII processing locations and sub-processors. SASE PoPs within the EU and EU-only log storage are now a standard tender requirement. |
| **Regulation**               | NIS2 (in force Oct 2024) raises security and supply-chain obligations for essential/important entities; EU 5G Toolbox — the Commission considers Member State decisions to restrict Huawei/ZTE justified; Cyber Resilience Act obligations phase in from 2026–2027.   |
| **Enterprise adoption**      | Cisco #1; HPE Aruba strong (DE, UK, NL, Nordics); Juniper strong in SP and finance; Extreme strong in UK public sector/education; Fortinet #1 in firewall units; Huawei material in some southern/eastern EU enterprises but declining in critical sectors.         |
| **Telecom**                  | Nokia and Ericsson dominate RAN/IP; Cisco and Juniper in core/edge routing; Ciena and Nokia/Infinera in optical.                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Data center**              | Arista and Cisco lead; Juniper Apstra and Nokia SR Linux/EDA gaining in sovereign cloud and SP DCs.                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Local support / partners** | Dense partner networks for Cisco, HPE, Fortinet, Palo Alto; country-specific depots generally provide 4-hr coverage in major cities.                                                                                                                                  |
| **Cost competitiveness**     | Fortinet and Extreme are frequently lowest in public tenders; Cisco wins on standardisation and skills; labour costs (~80% of US) make AIOps savings material.                                                                                                        |

### Country-specific notes

- **Germany:** strict works-council and data-protection reviews for
  cloud management; preference for on-prem options (Catalyst Center,
  Aruba Central On-Premises, Apstra).

- **UK:** Huawei removal from 5G by 2027; public sector frameworks
  (Crown Commercial Service) favour multiple vendors.

- **France:** SecNumCloud qualification increasingly requested for
  SASE/cloud services in public and critical sectors.

- **Nordics/Netherlands:** high cloud-management adoption; strong
  Juniper/Arista presence in SP and DC.

## United States

| **Dimension**               | **Assessment**                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-----------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **USD pricing**             | Reference market for global list prices; strongest public reseller pricing transparency (CDW, SHI, Connection, Insight).                                                                                              |
| **Sales tax**               | State/local 0–~10%; many enterprises are exempt or self-assess use tax; tariffs in 2025–2026 added surcharges on some imported hardware (e.g., Ubiquiti 'surcharge incl.' pricing: Pro Max 48 PoE $1,299 → $1,401). |
| **Enterprise adoption**     | Cisco dominant; HPE Aruba + Juniper is the principal campus challenger; Extreme strong in education/SLED; Meraki very strong mid-market.                                                                              |
| **Data center**             | Arista leads cloud titan and high-end enterprise DC; Cisco Nexus/ACI strong in enterprise; NVIDIA Spectrum-X a new entrant in AI back-end fabrics.                                                                    |
| **Cloud**                   | AWS/Azure/GCP native networking + Aviatrix/Alkira for multi-cloud; SASE from Zscaler, Palo Alto, Netskope, Cisco, Fortinet, Cato.                                                                                     |
| **Government**              | FedRAMP, TAA, NDAA §889 (prohibits Huawei/ZTE), Common Criteria, FIPS 140-3: Cisco, Juniper, Arista, HPE, Palo Alto, Fortinet hold broad certifications.                                                              |
| **Healthcare**              | Cisco, HPE Aruba, Juniper Mist, Extreme; HIPAA-driven segmentation and NAC (ISE/ClearPass).                                                                                                                           |
| **Financial services**      | Cisco, Arista (low-latency trading), Juniper, Palo Alto, Zscaler.                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Telecom**                 | Cisco, Juniper (HPE), Nokia, Ciena, Arista; Huawei/ZTE excluded under FCC rip-and-replace.                                                                                                                            |
| **Support & partners**      | Largest partner density and depot coverage for all US vendors.                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Pricing competitiveness** | Highest absolute labour cost makes operational efficiency (AIOps, automation) the dominant TCO lever.                                                                                                                 |

| **Europe**        | Confirm EU data residency for cloud management and SASE logs; NIS2 supply-chain clauses; WEEE; country VAT treatment; local-language support.                                                              |
| **United States** | Check tariff surcharges on hardware; TAA/NDAA §889 compliance for public sector; state sales-tax exemptions; leverage reseller competition (CDW, SHI, Insight).                                            |

author: Rupesh Kumar
content:
The previous five parts covered the market, products, licensing, cost and regional fit. This final part turns that into decisions: how the vendors score, which to choose for which job, how to move off Cisco safely, and how to buy without being caught out at renewal.

> **Key takeaways**
> - **Cisco (8.10)** and **Fortinet (8.05)** top the weighted scorecard, followed by **HPE Aruba (7.85)** and **Juniper (7.80)**.
> - For a new enterprise network today: **HPE or Cisco for campus/WLAN/NAC, Arista for the data center, Fortinet or Palo Alto for security/SD-WAN/SASE** — on a standards-based design.
> - **Negotiate renewals, not just the first purchase:** cap escalations, co-term everything and avoid true-forward clauses.

## Weighted vendor scorecard

## Migration playbook

### What makes a migration hard

| **Driver**                | **Low complexity**            | **High complexity**                                                        |
|---------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Proprietary protocols** | OSPF/BGP/IS-IS everywhere     | EIGRP, PVST+, VTP, SGT/TrustSec, ACI contracts                             |
| **Security integration**  | Standalone NAC/firewall       | ISE-driven dynamic segmentation, Stealthwatch, Umbrella tie-ins            |
| **Operations tooling**    | Generic NMS/SNMP, Ansible     | Catalyst Center templates, Meraki-specific APIs, SolarWinds custom scripts |
| **Skills**                | Teams with multi-vendor certs | CCNP-only teams, no automation                                             |
| **Contracts**             | Support co-terminating soon   | EA/ELA with true-forward; long DNA subscriptions                           |

### A six-step approach

1. **Discover:** inventory devices, licences, contract end-dates,
    proprietary features (EIGRP, TrustSec, VTP).

2. **Normalise:** migrate EIGRP → OSPF/BGP, PVST+ → MSTP, and SGT →
    standards-based (VXLAN-GBP / RADIUS VLAN) before swapping hardware.

3. **Pilot:** one branch + one campus building; validate NAC, wireless
    roaming, QoS, multicast.

4. **Phase by refresh cycle:** replace at EoL or contract expiry to
    avoid paying twice; keep Cisco core during access-layer migration
    (interop is standards-based).

5. **Retrain and automate:** budget 5–10% of capex for training and
    automation (Ansible/Terraform) to realise the opex savings modelled.

6. **Exit cleanly:** confirm Smart Account licence termination,
    return-to-vendor credits, and data-wipe certificates.

Typical migration professional-services cost: 10–20% of new hardware
value for campus, 15–25% for DC/SD-WAN; duration 3–6 months (campus of
500 users) to 18–36 months (global enterprise).

## Procurement playbook

### RFP structure

1. Issue a scenario-based RFP (like Scenarios A–D) and require a
    **5-year TCO** with every element priced separately: hardware,
    perpetual licences, term subscriptions, cloud management, security
    subscriptions, NAC, SASE, support, optics, services, training.

2. Require **list price, discount % and net price** per line, per
    region (INR/EUR/USD), excluding and including GST/VAT.

3. Demand **renewal price caps** (CPI or ≤5% per year) for all
    subscriptions and support for Years 2–7.

4. Require **co-termination** of all subscriptions and an annual
    true-up (not true-forward) mechanism.

5. Ask for **third-party optics support** or a fixed optics price list.

6. Evaluate with a weighted scoring model (like the scorecard above) and a hands-on
    **proof of concept** (minimum 30 days).

### Negotiation levers

- Competitive tension: at least three shortlisted vendors (e.g., Cisco,
  HPE, Fortinet) per domain.

- Quarter-end/fiscal-year-end timing (Cisco FY ends late July; HPE late
  October; Fortinet/Palo Alto vary).

- Competitive displacement and Make-in-India/PMA incentives (India).

- Bundle security + networking for platform discounts, but avoid
  committing beyond realistic device counts.

- Multi-year prepay only with price protection and
  termination-for-convenience on cloud services.

## Top 10 takeaways for network architects and procurement managers

1. **The market has consolidated:** HPE now owns Juniper (July 2025)
    and Arista owns VeloCloud (July 2025); re-baseline any vendor
    shortlists written before mid-2025.

2. **Hardware is the smallest part of TCO** above branch size —
    subscriptions, support, SASE/NAC and labour dominate 5-year cost.

3. **Cisco remains the lowest-risk choice** but typically costs 25–45%
    more over five years than the cheapest enterprise-grade stack (and
    ~15–18% more than HPE).

4. **HPE Networking is the most complete Cisco alternative;** insist on
    roadmap commitments and price protection during the Aruba–Juniper
    integration.

5. **Arista is the default DC benchmark;** pair it with a security
    vendor because it has no first-party NGFW.

6. **Fortinet delivers the lowest TCO for secure branches and SD-WAN,**
    but run a disciplined patch programme for FortiOS edge devices.

7. **SASE is converging with SD-WAN;** single-vendor SASE (Palo Alto,
    Fortinet, Cato, Netskope, Cisco, HPE) simplifies operations — test
    PoP coverage in India and the EU.

8. **Huawei is technically strong and cheap, but regulatory exposure**
    (US NDAA, EU 5G Toolbox, India trusted source) makes it unsuitable
    for most multinational and regulated buyers.

9. **Negotiate renewals, not just the first purchase:** cap
    escalations, co-term everything, and avoid true-forward clauses.

10. **Design for portability:** standards-based protocols (OSPF/BGP,
    EVPN-VXLAN, RADIUS, gNMI) and automation (Terraform/Ansible) reduce
    lock-in and make future competition credible.
